Mudcatca has the answer. Your question of the validity of anonymity also has a simple answer.

Yes. We are "anonymous". However, our brain does not like anonymity. It strives to make connections, to associate certain people with certain things. However anonymous you believe you are, you still form a connection with your community through your handle. You are TAThatBoomerang. In my mind, you are no longer anonymous. You have a personality, thoughts, form connections with others through that name. I might not know your name is Ted, IRL, but that hardly matters.

Smaller communities form stronger bonds with each other because they communicate more often. The stronger the bond, the less likely you are to be an asshole to somebody. This largely disappears in a bigger community, because I don't know you and simply do not care. You are more anonymous to me, and that makes you less of a person which puts my brain into the mindset of "Well, fuck this guy."
Smaller internet communities have less people so it's easier to get to know everyone and when someone is an asshole, everyone gangs up on them rather than other assholes who are lurking, joining in.
Smaller, therefore less people and, maybe, less assholes?

Smaller communities tend to attract those of special or unusual interests. People with such interests tend to be a little more open minded and mindful and respectful of personal differences than the mainstream - which swallows and regurgitates mass thought without digestion. Furthermore, mainstream people want mainstream ideas and reject nonconformity...thus their happy placement within the mainstream.

When a small community grows large (Reddit), the mainstream floods the borders like packs of Syrian refugees and by sheer numbers eventually overwhelm the smaller community's more genial members. Those members eventually become refugees themselves and must search out another small haven in which to establish themselves. And the circle of life continues.

People have a limited capacity to connect, care about and relate to other people. In a smaller community, we may recognize posters more frequently, get a feel for who they are, what they're about, and this engages more of our capacity to see them as people, and to feel a connection to them. Whereas on a larger site you're less likely to see any but the most obsessive power users with great regularity, and so the masses remain largely abstract to you.

If it is sensitive subject matter, the thought police are more interested in larger communities, so they will attempt to hide your communication with downvotes etc with greater veracity in larger communities. People who frequent these communities are aware of what is tolerated and what is berated, and wont waste too much time on what they perceive is any inevitably berated side of the discussion.
